questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How Hiroshima was rebuilt after the Second World War
The science and politics behind the atomic bomb
Why chemistry teachers use the periodic table
How Japan and the US became friends after the war
questions.why: Rob says they'll look into the science and the politics of The Manhattan Project.

questions.q: What happened after the bomb was dropped on Hiroshima?
options: Japan didn't give up, so Nagasaki was bombed
Japan surrendered on that very same day
The US decided not to use any more bombs
Germany dropped a bomb on the US in return
questions.why: Sam says when Japan refused to surrender, a second bomb was dropped on Nagasaki three days later.

questions.q: Before the war, what was the big challenge for scientists studying uranium?
options: Finding enough uranium in the ground to study
Making uranium heavier than other metals
Proving that uranium had any energy inside it
Releasing its energy in a controlled way
questions.why: Sam says the challenge was learning how to unleash its potential energy in a controlled way.

questions.q: What did scientists discover in 1938, according to Professor Frank Close?
options: Uranium atoms are very hard to damage
Uranium turns into water when it is heated
An atom splits in two when hit by a neutron
Neutrons are heavier than uranium atoms
questions.why: He says if you almost touched uranium with a single neutron, it would break apart, split in two.

questions.q: How much energy does splitting uranium release?
options: A billion times more than a chemical reaction
About the same as a normal chemical reaction
Twice as much as burning the same amount of coal
Less than scientists had first expected
questions.why: Sam says fission released a billion times more energy than a normal chemical reaction.

questions.q: Why does splitting uranium create a chain reaction?
options: Because the uranium gets hotter and hotter
Because more uranium is added each time
Because the energy makes the atoms move faster
Each split frees neutrons that hit more atoms
questions.why: Rob says splitting atoms releases two more neutrons, which hit more uranium, making four, then eight, and so on.

questions.q: What did Peierls and Frisch fear, according to Frank Close?
options: Britain would lose its scientists to the US
Germany might already be building one
The bomb would be too dangerous to test
Nobody would believe their discovery
questions.why: Their memorandum said it was conceivable Germany was developing the weapon, and the only defence was to have one.

questions.q: What 'strange twist of history' does Sam mention?
options: Hitler had built many bombs but never used them
Roosevelt never read the scientists' report
Hitler hadn't been building atomic bombs at all
Peierls and Frisch later worked for Germany
questions.why: Sam says, 'it turned out that Hitler hadn't been building atomic bombs at all'.
